title: Ruling 2026-01: Taxpayer's Conveyance of Parcels to LLC for Which it is Sole Member
text:
Date: February 23, 2026

Written by: Will S. Baker, Assistant Attorney General

Approved by: William C. Shouldice, IV, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your client [Company] regarding the Vermont Property Transfer Tax treatment of a transaction described below. This ruling is based on your representations communicated in your letter dated [date] and email dated [date].

Facts 

1. Your client [Company] (“Taxpayer” herein) owns three parcels in the State of Vermont. One is a residential rental property, and the other two are adjacent parcels to be combined into a single commercial parcel. The Taxpayer is the sole owner of these three parcels.

2. Taxpayer will convey or has conveyed all three parcels to a single limited liability company. The Taxpayer is the sole member of the LLC – there are no other owners.

Discussion 

You asked whether Taxpayer’s conveyance of its parcels to an LLC for which it is the sole member would incur Vermont Property Transfer Tax. These transactions are not subject to Property Transfer Tax.

The Property Transfer Tax is a tax upon the transfer by deed or transfer of a controlling interest of property within the State. 32 V.S.A. § 9602. However, there are exceptions to the tax. One such exemption is for transfers to effectuate a mere change of form of ownership, where there is no change in beneficial ownership. 32 V.S.A. 9603(6).

In this case, the Taxpayer is the sole owner of the three parcels being transferred. The transfer is from Taxpayer to an LLC, and the Taxpayer is the sole member of the LLC. Taxpayer remains the beneficial owner of the three parcels. For this reason, there is no change in beneficial ownership and the three transfers are exempt from Property Transfer Tax.

title: Ruling 2025-03: Sales of Parking Permits Not Subject to Sales and Use Tax
text:
Date: October 1, 2025

Written by: Matthew Phillips, Assistant Attorney General

Approved by: William C. Shouldice, IV, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for [Taxpayers] regarding the Vermont Sales and Use Tax treatment of parking permits sold through third-party software. This ruling is based upon representations communicated in your emails dated [date] and [date].

Facts 

1. [Taxpayer] is a public corporation [deleted].

2. As part of its operations, [deleted] maintains parking lots and offers parking permits for sale to [customers].

3. [Taxpayer] intends to utilize a third-party vendor's software to process parking permit transactions and payments electronically. [Customers] will purchase the permit online and will receive a receipt of the transaction. Payments to [Taxpayer] will be made via a payment processor.

Discussion 

You asked whether [Taxpayer] 's sales of parking permits, as described above, are subject to Vermont Sales and Use Tax. These transactions are not subject to Vermont Sales and Use Tax.

Vermont Sales and Use Tax applies to retail sales made in Vermont. 32 V.S.A. §§ 9771, 9773. "Retail sale" includes any sale, lease, or rental for a consideration for any purpose other than for resale, sublease, or subrent. 32 V.S.A. § 9701(5), (4)(A); Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(5)-1.

Only certain types of retail sales are subject to Vermont Sales and Use Tax. The types of retail sales subject to Vermont Sales and Use Tax are listed in 32 V.S.A. § 9771. Vermont Sales and Use Tax most commonly applies to sales or leases of tangible personal property, not real

property. 32 V.S.A. § 9771(1); Vt. Reg. 1.9701(5)-1. Vermont Sales and Use Tax also applies to sales of certain services (e.g., admissions to places of entertainment; telecommunications services). 32 V.S.A. § 9771(4)&(5).

None of the categories listed in Section 9771 apply to the rental of parking spaces. Parking spaces are not tangible personal property for purposes of Vermont's Sales and Use Tax; nor is the rental of parking spaces a taxable service. It is more akin to the rental of real property,

which is not subject to the Sales and Use Tax. Therefore, the transactions described above are not subject to Vermont's Sales and Use Tax.

title: Ruling 2024-08: Use of File Transfer and Digital Signing Software but Not Tax Preparation Software Subject to Sales Tax
text:
Date: December 16, 2024

Written by Abby Shepard

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling in response to your request of [date], regarding the Vermont Sales and Use Tax treatment of certain purchases made by your Firm. This ruling is based upon representations in your letter dated [date].

Facts 

1. You operate an accounting firm in Vermont. You use the purchases described below in the State.

[Company] 

2. [Company] is a large provider of human resources management services, allowing a business owner or manager to outsource human resources and payroll functions. ([website deleted]).

3. You utilize the payroll processing services of [Company]. It prepares payroll and executes payments to the employees of your firm, calculates and withholds income withholding, and prepares filings and remits filings and payments to the State and Federal Governments. It also provides you with reporting, payroll journals and tax reports.

4. [Company] charges you a monthly fee to perform these services.

5. You interact with [Company] and send and receive information between you and [Company] primarily via its website.

File Transfer and digital signing software 

6. You purchase and utilize software which enables your clients to upload documents and files to your computer systems. You use this software to receive the information for the purpose of tax preparation. You also use this software to obtain digital signatures from your clients and to share documents with your clients.

7. This is prewritten software and you have purchased this product “canned.” That is, the vendor of this software has neither written it for you nor customized it for you in any way and sells the same software to many customers.

Tax preparation 

8. For some clients, you provide tax return and financial statement preparation using the file transfer and digital signing software described above. Your interactions with your clients include interactions via the software, including the sharing of documents and collecting digital signatures.

Discussion 

You have asked whether the use of [Company]’s services and the use of the file transfer and digital signing software is subject to sales tax. [Company] provides a service to you and this service is not taxable in Vermont. Your use of the file transfer and digital signing software is subject to sales tax.

You also ask whether your tax return and financial statement preparation is subject to sales tax. This is a service that is not taxable in Vermont, even if you utilize taxable software to assist you in providing these services.

Vermont sales tax applies to retail sales within the State of prescribed items, including tangible personal property. 32 V.S.A. § 9771(1). Few services are subject to sales tax in Vermont and the services that are taxable do not relate to the services described in this ruling.

For retail sales, the tax applies to the sales price – the total amount of consideration paid. 32 V.S.A. § 9701(4)(A). Tangible personal property includes “prewritten computer software regardless of the method in which the prewritten computer software is paid for, delivered, or accessed.” 32 V.S.A. § 9701(7).

“Prewritten computer software” means “computer software, including prewritten upgrades, which is not designed and developed by the author or other creator to the specifications of a specific purchaser. The combining of two or more prewritten computer software programs or prewritten portions thereof does not cause the combination to be other than prewritten computer software. […].” Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(7)-2(A).

While you interact with [Company] primarily via its website, it is providing a service to you of preparing and calculating the payroll and withholdings of your employees, as well as executing the payments and preparing and filing the tax returns on your behalf with the Federal and State Governments. These tasks are specifically customized to your and your employees’ circumstances based on your needs and directions to [Company], utilizing the expertise of [Company] and provided on an ongoing basis. This is a service and is not subject to sales tax in Vermont.

The file transfer and digital signing software is prewritten software and the use of this software is subject to sales tax. This software is canned – it is the same software sold to many other customers. The software accomplishes the same tasks for all purchasers. The software is only beneficial for you if you specifically use and direct the software each instance to assist you in accomplishing the desired task, such as receiving a file or collecting a signature.

The provision of tax return and financial statement preparation is not subject to sales tax. This is a service; it is provided based on your specialized knowledge and skill and the delivered product is uniquely created for each client. Even though you may use various software programs to aid in the provision of these services, this does not make the service taxable.

title: Ruling 2024-04: Credit for Tax Paid on Long-Term Disability Insurance Payment Later Repaid to Insurance Company
text:
Date: August 19, 2024

Written by: Abby Shepard

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your clients [Taxpayers] (“the Taxpayer”) regarding credits available against the Vermont personal income tax. This ruling is based upon representations in your letter dated [date], with attached materials, and the updated Special Power of Attorney dated [date].

Facts 

1. In tax year 2022, the Taxpayer received a long-term disability insurance payment. The Taxpayer reported the payment as income and paid federal and State income tax on the payment in tax year 2022.

2. In tax year 2023, the Taxpayer was required by the insurance company to repay a portion of the long-term disability insurance payment.

Discussion 

You asked if Vermont law allows taxpayers to take a deduction or credit against Vermont personal income tax for repayment of long-term disability insurance income under a claim of right. No, the Taxpayer cannot take a deduction or credit for repayment of income under a claim of right against Vermont personal income tax, because Vermont law does not conform to the federal claim of right law nor does Vermont law offer a state deduction or credit.

The federal deduction or credit for repayment of income under a claim of right is codified under I.R.C. § 1341. For federal tax purposes, if a taxpayer properly reports income on a prior year’s tax return that in a later tax year is determined to have been paid in error and thus has to be repaid because the taxpayer was not in fact legally entitled to the income, and the amount repaid exceeds $3,000, then the taxpayer may be able to claim either a deduction or a credit against the taxpayer’s federal income tax. I.R.C. § 1341. A taxpayer may be able to deduct the amount repaid in the year of repayment on the federal Schedule A (Form 1040), line 16 as an “other itemized deduction.” Alternatively, a taxpayer may be able to take a credit against the taxpayer’s federal tax liability in the year of repayment on the federal Schedule 3 (Form 1040), line 13(b). A taxpayer may choose whichever method results in less federal tax owed. It is unclear from the facts provided whether the Taxpayer has claimed or received a federal deduction or credit for repayment of income under a claim of right.

Vermont income tax law adopts the U.S. statutes relating to the federal income tax, but without regard to federal income tax rates, for the purpose of computing Vermont tax liability. 32 V.S.A. § 5824. This means that federal income tax statutes apply unless Vermont law expressly adopts a different treatment. In the case of Vermont personal income tax, tax is imposed for each taxable year on the taxable income earned or received that year by every individual, if the income is subject to income taxation under federal law. 32 V.S.A. § 5822(a).

Vermont “taxable income” is defined as federal adjusted gross income (AGI) with certain additions and subtractions. 32 V.S.A. § 5811(21). Through this definition, Vermont law adopts the definition of federal AGI as its starting point for calculating Vermont taxable income. This means that any federal deductions or adjustments used after calculating federal AGI to determine federal taxable income are not part of Vermont taxable income. An example of a calculation that is not included in federal AGI is a federal itemized deduction. The federal deduction for repayment under a claim of right is an itemized deduction, therefore it is calculated after federal AGI and does not impact Vermont taxable income. I.R.C. §§ 62 and 1341. Accordingly, Vermont law does not recognize the federal deduction for repayment under a claim of right under I.R.C. § 1341 through conformity to federal income tax statutes.

Vermont law allows specifically listed addbacks and deductions from federal AGI to calculate Vermont taxable income. 32 V.S.A. § 5811(21). However, there is no specific deduction from Vermont taxable income for repayment of income under a claim of right. Id. As a result, Vermont law does not provide a state deduction for repayment of income under a claim of right.

Once a taxpayer’s taxable income is determined, it is multiplied by the applicable tax rate to calculate a taxpayer’s Vermont income tax liability. Vermont law then provides certain state-specific credits against tax owed. These credits include the credit for the elderly or permanently totally disabled and the Vermont child tax credit, among many others. See, 32 V.S.A. chapter 151, subchapter 2. Some of these credits expressly conform to certain aspects of federal income tax law. However, Vermont law does not provide a state income tax credit for repayments under a claim of right that conforms to or replicates the federal credit under I.R.C. § 1341. Accordingly, no income tax credit is available to the Taxpayer under Vermont law for repayment of long-term disability insurance income under a claim of right.

title: Ruling 2024-03: Sales Tax Applicability to Sales of DNA-Based Ancestry and Health History Reports
text:
Date: July 16, 2024

Written by: Abby Shepard

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your client [Taxpayer], regarding the Vermont sales and use tax and corporate income tax. This ruling is based upon representations in your letter dated [Date], including the attached PA-1 power of attorney form.

Facts 

1. [Taxpayer] is a [State]-based company with a distribution center in [State 2] and a specimen-processing laboratory in [State 3]. [Taxpayer] sells its services to both foreign and domestic customers, including customers in Vermont.

2. [Taxpayer] is in the business of selling ancestry and health history reports to customers based on [Taxpayer’s] analysis of DNA in customers’ saliva specimens. Customers order and pay for [Taxpayer’s] services online. [Taxpayer] mails a saliva kit from the [State 2] distribution center to the customer. The customer collects their own saliva specimen using the kit and mails the kit to the laboratory in [State 3]. The laboratory processes the specimen and generates an ancestry and health history report. The customer then accesses their individualized report through [Taxpayer’s] website.

3.The cost of the specimen-collecting kit is generally less than $1.00. The cost of the saliva specimen processing and analysis and the generation of an ancestry and health history report is generally $99.00. The use of the kit is integral to the provision of the service and is consumed in providing the service.

Discussion 

Sales and Use Tax 

1) Type of transaction 

You asked whether the Vermont sales and use tax applies to [Taxpayer’s] sales of DNA-based ancestry and health history reports to Vermont customers. [Taxpayer’s] sales are nontaxable because they include taxable and nontaxable products, and the purchase or sales price of the taxable products is de minimis.

Vermont law imposes sales and use tax on retail sales of tangible personal property in Vermont, unless an exemption applies. 32 V.S.A. §§ 9771, 9773. “Tangible personal property” (TPP) means “personal property that may be seen, weighed, measured, felt, touched, or in any other manner perceived by the senses.” 32 V.S.A. § 9701(7). Although some services are taxable in Vermont, such as admission to places of entertainment and certain telecommunications services, most services are not taxable. 32 V.S.A. §§ 9771, 9773. [Taxpayer’s] services are not of a type that is taxable under Vermont law. [Taxpayer’s] services can only be provided if the customer uses a physical specimen-collecting kit, however, which is taxable TPP when sold at retail, unless an exemption applies.

Under the Vermont sales and use tax rule, “[a] bundled transaction is the retail sale of two or more products, except real property and services to real property, where (1) the products are otherwise distinct and identifiable, and (2) the products are sold for one non-itemized price.” Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3. As a general rule, “if any product included in the bundled transaction would be taxable if sold separately”, then “sales tax must be collected on the selling price of a bundled transaction.” Id. Based on the facts in your letter, it is not clear whether the sales price of [Taxpayer] products is itemized. To be itemized, the sales price must be separately identified on a binding sales document like a receipt. If [Taxpayer’s] transactions are itemized, then the price of the TPP and the service price will not be bundled, and sales tax will only apply to the kit as TPP. If [Taxpayer’s] transactions are not itemized, then sales tax will apply to the entire bundled transaction unless an exception applies.

There are several exceptions to the general rule on bundled transactions that appear to apply to [Taxpayer’s] sales. First, as long as the price of the TPP (the kit) is de minimis, which means 10% or less of the total purchase price, then sales tax will not apply. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3(C)(3). Second, even if the value of the kit is not de minimis, if the true object of the transaction is a nontaxable service, then sales tax will not apply.

A transaction that otherwise meets the definition of a bundled transaction is not considered a bundled transaction if the transaction “includes taxable products and nontaxable products and the purchase price or sales price of the taxable products is de minimis.” Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3(C)(3); see also, 32 V.S.A. § 9741(35). “De minimis” means the seller’s purchase price or sales price of the taxable products is 10% or less of the total purchase price or sales price of the bundled products. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3(C)(3)(a); see also, 32 V.S.A. § 9741(35). A transaction that meets the conditions to be considered de minimis is not taxable. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3(C); see also, 32 V.S.A. § 9741(35). Based on the facts in your letter, [Taxpayer’s] sales include both taxable products (the kit as TPP) and nontaxable products (the report as a service). According to the facts provided, the purchase price or sales price of the taxable products is de minimis, because the kit is 10% or less (the kit’s price is $1.00, which represents 1%) of the total $100 purchase price or sales price of the bundled products. Therefore, [Taxpayer’s] sales would not be considered a bundled transaction and sales tax would not apply.

Even if the de minimis exception did not apply, a transaction that otherwise meets the definition of a bundled transaction is not considered a bundled transaction if the transaction is a retail sale of both (1) TPP and (2) a service; the TPP is essential to the use of the service; the TPP is provided exclusively in connection with the service; and the service is the true object of the transaction. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3(C)(1); see also, 32 V.S.A. § 9741(35). Based on the facts provided, [Taxpayer’s] retail sales include both TPP (the kit) and a service (the specimen-processing required to produce an ancestry and health history report). The TPP is essential to the use of the service and the TPP is provided exclusively in connection with the service, because the service can only be performed by using the specimen-collecting kit. Additionally, the service is the true object of the transaction, because the customer is paying for the information contained in the report, not for the kit. Therefore, [Taxpayer’s] sales would not be considered a bundled transaction and sales tax would not apply.

2) Location of transaction (situs) 

You asked whether Vermont law considers the sale to have occurred in [State 3], where the specimen-processing occurs, or in Vermont, where the customer receives the kit delivery and presumably uses the service. [Taxpayer’s] Vermont customers take possession of the kit in Vermont and first use services in Vermont, therefore the sale is sourced to Vermont.

The General Sourcing Rules determine whether a sale is sourced to Vermont. Vt. Reg. §§ 1.9701(8)-1–1.9701(8)-3. When the retail sale of product is not received by the purchaser at the seller’s business location, then the sale is sourced to the location where receipt by the purchaser occurs, including the location indicated by instructions for delivery to the purchaser known to the seller. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(8)-3(A)(2). Under the General Sourcing Rules, “receive” and “receipt” mean taking possession of tangible personal property or making first use of services. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(8)-2(1) and (2). Based on the facts in your letter, [Taxpayer’s] customers must provide instructions for delivery of the kits to the customer in order to collect DNA specimens to send to the [State 3] processing lab. Without a physical delivery address for the customer, then the service cannot be provided. If the instructions to deliver the kit to the customer indicate a location in Vermont, then the sales are sourced to Vermont. Additionally, according to the presumption stated in your letter, customers are making first use of the services in Vermont, so the sales are sourced to Vermont.

3) Use tax 

You asked whether [Taxpayer] owes Vermont use tax on DNA-collecting kits shipped from [State 2] to customers in Vermont. [Taxpayer] does not owe Vermont use tax on the kits to the extent that use tax has already been paid in [State 2] at a rate of at least 6% when [Taxpayer] ships the kits to Vermont customers.

Vermont law imposes a 6% compensating use tax on sales of TPP if the TPP will be used in Vermont, the TPP has not been or will not be subject to the Vermont sales tax, and the TPP is not otherwise exempt. 32 V.S.A. § 9773; Vt. Reg. § 1.9773. A relevant exemption exists for circumstances where retail sales or use tax on the TPP has been paid to another state or jurisdiction, if the other state or jurisdiction allows a corresponding exemption to Vermont’s, and if the other state or jurisdiction’s tax rate is the same or higher than Vermont 6% tax rate. 32 V.S.A. § 9744(a)(3). If Vermont’s tax rate is higher than the other state or jurisdiction’s tax rate, then Vermont tax applies to the extent of the difference in rates. Id. First, based on the facts in your letter, [Taxpayer] ships the kits from [State 2] to be used or consumed by [Taxpayer’s] customers in Vermont. Second, the kits will not be subject to the Vermont sales tax because they are part of a nontaxable sale. Third, [Taxpayer] paid use tax on the kits to [State 2], and [State 2] appears to allow a corresponding exemption to Vermont’s exemption. 32 V.S.A. § 9744(a)(3); U.C.A. § 59-12-104(26). In [State 2] it appears that the use tax rate can be lower than 6%, but depending on the local taxing jurisdiction, can also be much higher. Accordingly, depending on what rate of use tax [Taxpayer] paid in [State 2], [Taxpayer’s] use of the kits may be fully exempt from Vermont use tax or [Taxpayer] may owe use tax on the kits to the extent of the difference in Vermont and [State 2’s] tax rates.

Corporate Income Tax 

In addition to the issues raised in your letter, there may also be corporate income tax implications for the sales [Taxpayer] is making into Vermont. The statements of law provided below are for informational purposes only and do not constitute a position or interpretation taken by the Department on [Taxpayer’s] tax standing or liability. The Department would need a duly executed power of attorney form from [Taxpayer] authorizing us to communicate with you about any corporate income tax implications of sales made within Vermont.

Under Vermont corporate income tax law, a “taxable corporation” is defined in relevant part as a corporation that received any income allocable or apportionable to Vermont. 32 V.S.A. § 5811(15)(C). Taxable corporations are required to file a Vermont corporate income tax return and are subject to the greater of the income tax based on net income or the minimum corporate gross receipts tax. 32 V.S.A. § 5832(1) and (2). A taxable corporation that derives income from sales into Vermont and outside Vermont must apportion its income to Vermont by multiplying Vermont net income by the gross sales or charges for services performed within Vermont, expressed as a percentage of the sales or charges whether within or outside Vermont. Id. 32 V.S.A. § 5833(a). Sales are deemed to be made in Vermont if the corporation’s market for the sales is in Vermont (also called market-based sourcing). 32 V.S.A. § 5833(a)(2). In the case of the sale of a service, the corporation’s market is in Vermont if and to the extent that the service is delivered to a location in Vermont. 32 V.S.A. § 5833(a)(2)(C).

title: Ruling 2024-02: Vermont Sales and Use Tax on Sales Subject to a Company Rebate
text:
Date: March 25, 2024

Witten by: Abby Shepard

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for [Taxpayer] (“[Taxpayer]”) regarding Vermont sales and use tax on sales subject to a company rebate. This ruling is based on representations in your letter dated [date], and the attached exhibits.

Facts 

1. [Taxpayer] is a national retailer of [deleted] supplies to retail and wholesale customers. [Taxpayer] has [deleted] stores in Vermont doing business as [Company].

2. [Taxpayer] offers a volume rebate program to qualifying customers that is tiered from 1.25% to 2.5% of the customer’s total spending during the rebate accrual period. When a customer earns a rebate at the end of the accrual period, [Taxpayer] issues a rebate credit memo. The rebate is issued either as a credit reducing future purchases or as a cash payment to the customer. For example, if the customer spends $1,250,000.00 at the end of the calendar year when total spending is calculated, then the customer receives a 1.25% rebate on all purchases, which equals $15,625.00.

Discussion 

[Taxpayer] asked whether sales and use tax should be refunded to a customer if the customer receives a rebate. Yes, for the reasons stated below, sales tax must be refunded if [Taxpayer’s] rebate is based on purchases of taxable items. [Taxpayer] may then net the amount of refunded sales tax out of its tax remittance to the Department of Taxes in the following month.

Vermont imposes a 6% sales and use tax on the sales price charged for retail sales of tangible personal property in Vermont. 32 V.S.A. §§ 9771, 9773. Sales price means the total amount of consideration for which personal property or services are sold, but does not include discounts, including cash, term, or coupons that are allowed by a seller (not those reimbursed by a third party) and that are taken by a purchaser on a sale. 32 V.S.A. § 9701(4)(A), (4)(B)(i); Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–2(1). In other words, when a coupon or rebate is issued by the seller, the sales price on which tax is calculated is reduced accordingly, and less tax is owed by the purchaser as a result. In [Taxpayer’s] case, the rebate is only issued at the end of the accrual period after sales have already been made and tax has already been collected and remitted to the State. Given that the rebate reduces the sales price received by [Taxpayer], any sales tax owed by the purchaser on taxable products is reduced accordingly and should be refunded to the purchaser.

Vermont law makes sellers personally and individually liable for sales and use tax collection from purchasers and tax remittance to the State. 32 V.S.A. § 9703(a). For a seller to receive a refund or credit on sales and use tax payments to the State, the seller must first refund the purchaser for any tax that was erroneously collected. 32 V.S.A. §§ 9703(d), 9781(a); Vt. Reg. § 1.9781(A).

Vermont allows certain municipalities to impose a 1% local option tax on any sales that would be subject to the State sales tax. 24 V.S.A. § 138(c). Local option tax is determined based on the destination of the sale, which means where the purchaser receives the product. Id. The destination could be at the seller’s business location if that is where the product is received by the purchaser or the location where the product is delivered to the purchaser. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(8)-1–(8)-3. Burlington, South Burlington, and Williston are some examples of

Vermont municipalities that impose a 1% local option sales tax. [Taxpayer] should ensure that it is collecting and remitting the correct amount of State and local option sales taxes in the municipalities where it makes taxable sales.

In [Taxpayer’s] case, a customer receiving a rebate should also receive a refund of State sales tax and, where applicable, local option sales tax paid. The amount of the refunded tax will depend on whether the rebated sales were all taxable products or whether only some products were taxable and others were nontaxable. [Taxpayer] must also identify the municipality where any refunded local option tax was initially collected. If [Taxpayer]sells a combination of taxable and nontaxable products and delivers in different municipalities with different local option tax treatment, however, [Taxpayer]will need to do a detailed accounting of each transaction making up the rebated amount of purchases. The amount of taxes refunded must be based on the taxability of the products sold and rebated.

For example, if one of [Taxpayer’s] customer has spent $1,250,000.00 at the end of the calendar year and so qualifies for a 1.25% rebate ($15,625.00), and all of the customer’s purchases were taxable products, then the amount of the State sales tax to be refunded is 6% of the rebated amount ($15,625.00*0.06 = $937.50). If any local option tax was collected, then [Taxpayer]should refund its customer another 1% of the rebated amount ($15,625.00*0.01 = $156.25).

Once [Taxpayer] has established that its customers have been refunded the appropriate amount of tax paid, then the amount of refunded State sales tax and local option tax can be credited against [Taxpayer’s] next return and payment filed with the Department. [Taxpayer] should indicate the municipality or municipalities where the corresponding local option sales tax was collected.

title: Ruling 2023-03: Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement (ICHRA) Qualifies as "Health Care Coverage"
text:
Date: August 28, 2023

Written by: Emily Bergquist

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your company, [Taxpayer], Taxpayer, regarding whether an Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement qualifies as an offer of insurance for the purposes of the Health Care Fund Contribution Assessment. This ruling is based upon representations in your request letter received in this office [date].

Facts 

Your company proposes to offer an Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement for its employees. You ask whether this plan will qualify as “health care coverage” for purposes of your company’s employer liability under Vermont’s Health Care Fund contribution law. You have also asked for directions on completing the Department’s Health Care reporting forms.

Discussion 

Vermont law provides generally that an employer who does not offer “health care coverage” to its employees must pay a “Health Care Fund contribution” for each “uncovered employee” in excess of four employees. 32 V.S.A. § 10503(a).

You have asked whether an Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement (ICHRA) qualifies as “health care coverage” for purposes of the Health Care Fund contribution law.

Under an ICHRA, an employer reimburses its employees for a portion of their health care costs. To qualify as an ICHRA, the plan must meet the requirements of the Federal ICHRA provisions. See, Health Reimbursement Arrangements and Other Account-Based Group Health Plans, 84 FR 28888-01, 2019 WL 2524535(F.R.).

“Health care coverage” is defined in the Vermont statute as “any private or public plan that includes both hospital and physician services.” 32 V.S.A. § 10502(4). There is no further definition of “health care coverage” in the statute. The Department of Taxes (Department) has stated in its publication “Guide to the Health Care Fund Contribution Assessment” that the health care coverage law “requires an employer to pay for part of a plan but does not specify how much it must pay. Thus, any amount paid by the employer is acceptable for an employee to be considered covered.” Id., p. 4. The only other statutory requirement is that the “plan” that is paid for must provide coverage for “both hospital and physician services.”

Given the wide latitude provided in the Vermont statute, a qualified ICHRA plan provided to your employees would constitute “health care coverage,” so long as it results in payments by your company, as the employer, of any amount, for your employees’ private or public plans that cover “both hospital and physician services.”

Therefore, under Section 2 of the Department’s Health Care Contributions worksheet, Form HC-1, your offer of an ICHRA plan would qualify you as an employer who “offers to pay part or all of the cost of health care coverage” for your employees.

While your ICHRA will qualify as “health care coverage,” you will still owe a Health Care Contribution for “uncovered” employees. These include any employee who is (a) an employee of an employer who does not offer to pay any part of the cost of health care coverage for its employees; or (b) not eligible for the plan you offer; or (c) an employee who is offered the plan but elects not to accept the coverage and is enrolled in Medicaid; has no other health care coverage except Medicaid; or (c) who has purchased health insurance as an individual through the Vermont Health Benefit Exchange. 32 V.S.A. § 10502(7).

To determine whether your employees are “uncovered,” your employees must annually complete Form HC-2, Declaration of Health Care Coverage, and submit it to you.

You may then use the HC-1 worksheet to determine the number of health care contributions for which you may be liable. Your quarterly Health Care Contributions, if any, are reported on Form WHT-436.

title: Ruling 2023-01: Pump Truck Operated by Concrete Retailer is Nontaxable Service
text:
Date: July 6, 2023

Written by: Emily Bergquist

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your company, [Taxpayer], (Taxpayer), regarding the applicability of sales tax to sales of concrete, delivery charges and charges for use of Taxpayer’s pump truck. This ruling is based upon representations in your letter dated [date], received in this office [date], the letter of [individual], dated [date], and telephone conversations with [individual].

Ruling 

Based upon the facts presented, charges for your concrete pump truck are not subject to sales tax.

Facts 

Taxpayer is a Vermont business that [deleted]. Taxpayer’s customers are contractors who use the concrete to improve the real property of the contractor or the contractor’s customer.

When a customer has contracted for a purchase of concrete, Taxpayer delivers the concrete to the customer’s site in one of its mixer trucks.

A mixer truck has a rotating drum that mixes the concrete during transportation. Constant mixing of the concrete is necessary to prevent the concrete from setting before it is delivered.

Once at the customer’s site, the mixer truck discharges the concrete directly from the truck’s mixer drum onto the desired location, directing the flow by means of a chute or trough or slide attached to the mixer truck.

For smaller amounts of concrete, the customer may then convey the concrete from the delivery site by wheelbarrow to the forms being used to place the concrete.

In some cases, the mixer truck may discharge concrete into a large bucket which is then lifted by a crane to higher elevations or over obstacles, where the crane operator controls the pouring of concrete from the bucket to place the concrete.

In cases where concrete must be moved from the delivery site a greater distance, the mixer truck may discharge its concrete onto a conveyor belt or platform, which moves the concrete over the longer horizontal or vertical distance to where the concrete is to be placed.

In addition to its mixer trucks, Taxpayer operates concrete pump trucks which a customer may request for use in placing the concrete in the desired area of the customer’s building site. The mixer truck in that case will transport the concrete to the customer’s construction site and there discharge the concrete into the pump truck operated by Taxpayer’s employee. A pump truck is not used for transport of concrete to the customer’s job site, and use of the pump truck is completely optional. Once concrete is discharged from the mixer truck into the pump truck, the pump truck pumps the concrete horizontally or vertically through a hose, to place the concrete as required. A customer may request a pump truck because it saves the customer the labor costs of manual placing concrete and ensures accurate measurement of the amount of concrete to be placed in forms at the construction site. The customer is charged separately for the pump truck and its operation.

You have asked whether Taxpayer must collect sales tax on the charge for the pump truck to place the concrete at the customer’s construction site.

Discussion 

Vermont sales tax is imposed at the rate of six percent (1) on the “sales price” of a “retail sale” of “tangible personal property” in Vermont. 32 V.S.A. § 9771.

Taxpayer’s customers are contractors who use the concrete to improve the real property of the contractor or contractor’s customers. A taxable “retail sale” includes a sale to a contractor for use in improving real property. 32 V.S.A. §9701(5). Taxpayer must therefore collect sales tax on its sales of concrete to contractors.

The “sales price” includes “delivery charges” and “charges by the seller for any services necessary to complete the sale, other than installation charges.” 32 V.S.A. § 9701(4)(A)(iii), (iv).

“Delivery charges” are for “delivery to a location designated by the purchaser . . . including, but not limited to, transportation, shipping, postage, handling, crating, and packing.” Vermont Department of Taxes Sales and Use Tax Regulations (Effective date: January 1, 2019) (“Reg.”) § 1.9701(4)-1. “If the seller elects not to allocate the delivery charge, the entire charge is subject to the tax.” Id. Here, Taxpayer charges the customer a single sales price for the concrete and delivery of the concrete in its mixer truck. That single sales price is subject to sales tax.

Once at the site, the mixer truck discharges the concrete at the area “designated by the purchaser.” The customer directs where the concrete must be discharged; for example, onto the ground, into a wheelbarrow, into a crane bucket, or into a waiting pump truck, whether that pump truck is the customer’s or is Taxpayer’s pump truck requested by the customer. The discharge completes delivery of the concrete.

Use of Taxpayer’s pump truck is a separate transaction from the sale and delivery of the concrete. A pump truck is never used to transport (deliver) concrete to the job site. Rental of Taxpayer’s pump truck and operator is completely optional; it is not a “service necessary to complete the sale” of the concrete. The pump truck is machinery used to place concrete after the concrete has been delivered to the job site. The charge for the pump truck and operator is therefore not included as a “delivery charge” in the taxable “sales price” of the concrete.

Nor is rental of Taxpayer’s pump truck and operator itself a taxable transaction. A taxable “lease or rental” is “any transfer of possession or control of the tangible personal property.” Reg. § 1.9701(5)-2. Taxpayer does not transfer possession or control of the pump truck to its customer; Taxpayer retains possession and control of the truck at all times, so this is not a taxable lease or rental. And specifically, a taxable “lease or rental” excludes “providing tangible personal property along with an operator for a fixed or indeterminate period of time [where] the operator is necessary for the equipment to perform as designed.” Reg. § 1.9701(5)-2.A.3.

As a result, the separate charge for the pump truck is not subject to sales tax.

title: Ruling 2022-07: Renter Credit; Disabled Adult Receiving Social Security and Has Shared Living Provider
text:
Date: January 5, 2023

Written by: Emily Bergquist

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your client, [Taxpayer] (Claimant), regarding the availability of the renter credit for rent paid for his homeshare residence. This ruling is based upon representations in your email dated [date].

Facts 

1. Claimant is a developmentally disabled adult, collecting Social Security Disability, and living with a shared living home provider, paying the room and board rate set by Vermont Department of Disabilities, Aging and Independent Living.

2. Room and board for Claimant includes a bedroom, electricity, heat, bathroom, and meals and is the primary residence of Claimant. He has no other home to live in. He is not able to care for himself or live alone.

3. A shared living home provider receives room and board income from Claimant, and also a stipend for services from a mental health agency in Vermont that is paid from a Medicaid waiver.

Discussion 

You have asked whether a developmentally disabled adult, who is collecting Social Security Disability payments, and living with a shared living home provider, may claim a renter credit.

A qualified low-income individual who rents his primary residence may be eligible for a rental credit of up to $2500. 32 V.S.A. § 6066(b). The credit calculation is based on the income level of the renter and either (a) the rent paid (if the individual receives a rental subsidy) or (b) a

statutory calculation involving “fair market rent” as defined in federal law, if the individual does not receive a rental subsidy. Id.

There is nothing in the statute that would prohibit per se a developmentally disabled adult, who is collecting Social Security Disability payments, and living with a shared living home provider, from claiming the renter credit. (1) If the renter meets the low-income limitations of the statute, he is eligible to apply. 32 V.S.A. § 6062(b)(1). If the renter receives a rental subsidy, the amount of credit available is calculated based on the amount of “rent” paid directly by Claimant from Claimant’s own funds.

“Rent” for purposes of the credit is defined to include only payments “to the extent that the payments are solely for the right of occupancy” of the residence. 32 V.S.A. § 6061(7)(B). This means “rent” does not include payments for electricity, heat, meals, or any item other than the space occupied by the renter. If any of these other items are included in the payments made by the renter, they must be subtracted from the payments to determine the amount qualified as “rent.” The agreement between the social services agency and the placement home or nursing home, often specifies the amount to be paid as rent. This agreement should be provided to the Department with the renter credit application.

In cases involving a rental subsidy, only the amount “actually paid by the individual” claimant may be included as “rent” for purposes of calculating the credit. 32 V.S.A. § 6061(7)(B). This means that any payments made from funds of any other person or entity, even though paid on behalf of Claimant, may not be counted as “rent” for the credit calculation. Moreover, payments made to a trust or guardian or other person or entity for the benefit of Claimant, and not paid directly to Claimant, are not money of the Claimant himself; therefore, payments made from these other sources are not payments “actually paid by the individual” renter, and do not constitute “rent” for calculation of the credit. However, payments made from Claimant’s own funds will qualify as “rent” even if a guardian or other person writes the check or otherwise transfers Claimant’s funds to the landlord.

There are additional limitations that may reduce or bar a renter credit claim. A claimant must have been domiciled in Vermont for the entire taxable year, must have rented for at least six calendar months (not necessarily consecutive), and may not be a person claimed as a dependent by any taxpayer for Federal income tax purposes. 32 V.S.A. § 6066(c). In addition, if a claimant receives a rental subsidy, the credit is limited to a maximum of ten percent of gross rent paid. 32 V.S.A. § 6066(b)(1)(D). If the claimant's income is greater than the “very low-income” limit, the claimant is not entitled to a renter credit. 32 V.S.A. § 6066(b)(1)(C). Details of how to calculate a claimant’s income and how to calculate the renter credit amount may be found in the Department’s instructions for the renter credit claim form, Form RCC-146.

Note that the amount of renter credit or property tax rebate available to the shared-living host may be affected by the fact that Claimant is sharing the household and by the amount of space rented to Claimant.

The prior law provided that a renter credit (formerly called a “renter rebate”) was based on 21 percent of “gross rent,” and “gross rent” was defined to exclude “payments made under a written homesharing agreement pursuant to a nonprofit homesharing program.” 32 V.S.A. § 6061(7). Beginning in 2021, that exclusion was removed from the law, with the result that payments made under such a homesharing program may be counted as gross rent if they otherwise qualify. 32 V.S.A. § 6061(7)(A), (B).

title: Ruling 2022-06: Vermont Resident Working in New Hampshire Has Not Abandoned Vermont Domicile
text:
Date: November 2, 2022

Written by: Emily Bergquist

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your client, [Taxpayer] (Taxpayer), regarding the applicability of Vermont income tax to her 2022 taxable income. This ruling is based upon representations in your letter dated [date].

Facts 

1. Taxpayer recently moved from Vermont to New Hampshire for a job that started on [date].

2. Taxpayer has rented a 2-bedroom, 2-bathroom apartment in [City], New Hampshire.

3. Taxpayer and her husband own a 3-bedroom, 2-bathroom home in [City], Vermont. Her husband plans to stay at the [City] house when he is in Vermont during the work week.

4. Taxpayer will spend most of her time in New Hampshire, including the entire work week as well as many weekends. She may travel to Vermont on some weekends and may travel to Vermont to visit family and friends or for vacations.

5. Most of Taxpayer’s personal possessions are in New Hampshire, including certain things that are near and dear to her like her jewelry, camera, video camera, and most of her photographs.

6. Taxpayer’s only job will be as an [position] at [workplace] in [City], New Hampshire. She will work in person at the office, as well as [numerous locations] in New Hampshire.

7. Taxpayer’s husband will be in New Hampshire 2 to 3 work days a week and on many weekends. He is employed by a Vermont-based company and will work in-person in Vermont approximately two to three days a week and work remotely from New Hampshire on the other

work days.

8. Taxpayer’s parents and siblings reside in Vermont and she has no children.

9. Taxpayer has registered her car in New Hampshire and plans to obtain a New Hampshire driver’s license by [date].

10. Taxpayer plans to register to vote in New Hampshire.

Discussion 

Vermont law of domicile 

Vermont income tax is imposed on all the income of every resident, and on income of every nonresident from sources within the State. 32 V.S.A. § 5822(a), (b). “Residency” is defined as follows:

(11) “Residency.”

(A) An individual qualifies for residency in this State for that portion of the taxable year during which:

(i) the individual is domiciled in this State; or

(ii) the individual maintains a permanent place of abode within this State if the individual both maintains a permanent place of abode and is present in this State for more than an aggregate of 183 days of that taxable year.

32 V.S.A. § 5811(11).

“Domicile” is defined in the Department’s income tax regulations:

Section 2 Definition of Domicile

(a) Domicile means the place where an individual has a true, fixed permanent home, and to which place, whenever the person is absent, he or she has the intention of returning. An individual may have several places of abode in a year, but at no time can he or she have more than one domicile. Domicile is not limited to a specific structure, but refers rather to a place or an area to which the individual expects to return. Department of Taxes Regulations (Eff. 8/06/04) (“Regs.”) §§ 1.5811(11)(A)(1), Sec. 2(a).

A husband and wife are presumed to have the same domicile:

It is presumed that the domiciles of a husband and wife . . . are the same, unless there is affirmative evidence to the contrary. However, spouses who are separated may acquire separate domiciles, even though no judgment or decree of separation has been rendered provided the requisite move and intent are present. Id. at Sec. 6.

Once established, a domicile is never lost unless there is both (1) a change to a new place of residence and (2) abandonment of the former residence. Id. at Sec. (2)(c).

Taxpayer bears the burden of proving a change of domicile by clear and convincing evidence. Id. at Sec. 5(a), (b). Intent to change domicile must be “manifested by unequivocal acts.” Id. at Sec. 5(b).

“The fact that a change of domicile was motivated primarily by a desire to gain a tax advantage is immaterial if the intention of the individual to acquire a new domicile is absolute and fixed and the actions of the individual confirm that intention.” Id. at Sec. 4(a).

“An individual who is in transit between old and new domiciles is domiciled in the old domicile until the new one is established.” Id. at Sec. 2(e).

The regulations describe factors to consider in determining a domicile:

Section 3 Relevant Factors

The factors which are deemed of primary relevance to a fair determination of an individual’s domicile are the facts and circumstances that are not readily changeable by the taxpayer in order to alter their domicile for tax reasons. The following factors, in no particular order, shall be considered in determining an individual’s domicile.

(a) Home. The Department will consider what residences are owned or rented (for the taxpayer’s use) by the taxpayer; where they are located; how they are used; and the sizes, values and uses of each residence.

(b) Time. The Department will consider where and how the individual spends time during the tax year; whether the taxpayer is retired or actively involved in a business or profession; how much the individual travels; the nature of the travel; where the individual spends time when not required to be at a location for employment reasons, and the overall pattern of residence of the individual.

(c) Items Near and Dear. The Department will consider where items or possessions that the individual considers “near and dear” to his or her heart are located, e.g. items of significant sentimental value, family heirlooms, collections of valuables or possessions that enhance the quality of the individual’s life.

(d) Active Business Involvement. The Department will consider how the individual earns a living; where the individual's place of employment is; whether the individual is actively involved in any business ownership or professions, and if so, the degree; where the business or professional office is located and the ;proportion of in-state to out-of-state business activities. “Actively involved” means the individual participates in the day-to-day operation, or in a policymaking position, of a business.

(e) Family Connections. The Department will consider where members of the individual’s immediate family reside; where minor children attend school, and the type of school facility. “Immediate family” means the spouse, civil union partner, child, or parent of an individual.

Other factors which may be considered include home address and legal residence listed on federal tax returns, place where the individual is registered to vote, place of vehicle registration, state of driver’s or professional license, place of club and organization memberships, place where mail is received. There may be other similar factors. However, because these factors may be altered without a true commitment to such location they will generally not carry as much weight as factors (a) through (e) above.

Id. at Sec. 3. In addition to these factors, several others are considered, particularly with regard

to a claimed change of domicile:

1. location of domicile for prior years;

2. registration as voter;

3. voting by absentee ballot;

4. place of filing of federal income tax returns;

5. filing and payment of state income taxes;

6. declaration of place of residence in will;

7. recitals in deeds and legal documents;

8. written and oral declarations generally;

9. situs of bank accounts and securities;

10. membership in churches, clubs, lodges, societies;

11. automobile registration and license;

12. claiming or filing homestead exemptions;

13. school attended by minor children.

Id. at Sec. 4(b). None of these factors are conclusive; they are weighed in view of all the facts. Id.

Application of the law to Taxpayer’s facts 

At least until [month] of this year, Taxpayer’s domicile was Vermont, her true, fixed permanent home where she owns a house and resides with her husband. Her Vermont domicile will not be lost unless she successfully changes her place of residence and takes unequivocal steps to abandon her Vermont domicile. Taxpayer must prove her change of domicile by clear and convincing evidence. See Quazzo v. Dep't of Taxes, 2014 VT 81 (2014).

The evidence presented does not support a finding that Taxpayer has changed her domicile to New Hampshire:

Home. Taxpayer owns a 3-bedroom, 2-bathroom house with her husband in Vermont; she has rented a 2-bedroom, 2-bathroom apartment in New Hampshire. Taxpayer’s ownership of the Vermont house, and the fact that the house is larger than an apartment she rents in New

Hampshire, weigh in favor of Vermont domicile.

Time. Taxpayer will spend the entire work week in New Hampshire, and most weekends. This weighs in favor of New Hampshire domicile.

Items near and dear. Taxpayer’s jewelry, camera, video camera, and most of her photographs are in her New Hampshire apartment. There is no evidence of what items Taxpayer keeps at her Vermont house, or where she keeps her important papers, family heirlooms, items of historical or sentimental value, or other significant personal items. This evidence is too incomplete to weigh in favor of either location.

Active business involvement. Taxpayer’s place of business is in New Hampshire. This weighs in favor of New Hampshire domicile.

Family connections. Taxpayer’s husband, parents and siblings live in Vermont. There is no evidence of New Hampshire relatives. This weighs in favor of Vermont domicile.

Miscellaneous other factors. Taxpayer will register her vehicle in New Hampshire, obtain a New Hampshire driver’s license and register to vote in New Hampshire. These facts weigh in favor of New Hampshire domicile. The regulations, however, state that these factors may be altered without a true commitment to location, and do not carry as much weight as other factors. It is not known whether Taxpayer has changed her address on various credit card and other accounts or will continue to receive mail at her Vermont address - factors which could weigh in favor of Vermont domicile.

It is not known what address Taxpayer will use for her Federal income tax returns, where she declares her place of residence in her will, if any, what address she will use on her credit card and other accounts, whether she will retain Vermont bank accounts, whether she will continue to see Vermont doctors and dentists, and whether she and her husband will declare their [City] house as a homestead (domicile) for purposes of [City] property tax. These are all indicia of domicile.

Of the known factors, two weigh in favor of New Hampshire: time spent in New Hampshire and location of her employment; two weigh in favor of Vermont domicile: the Vermont house and husband’s residence in the Vermont house. The New Hampshire car registration and

driver’s license and New Hampshire voter registration weigh in favor of New Hampshire domicile, but do not carry as much weight as the other factors. Continuing ownership of the Vermont house and the fact that her husband continues to reside there, coupled with the fact that Taxpayer intends to return there periodically to visit her husband, family and friends, indicate steps to abandon her Vermont domicile.

Since the intent to change domicile must be manifested by unequivocal acts, and since proof of change of domicile must be clear and convincing, the evidence here is insufficient to prove a change of domicile or to project a change of domicile for future years. Taxpayer’s domicile remains Vermont. Her New Hampshire salary will be subject to Vermont personal income tax.

title: Ruling 2022-05: Tax Applied to Transfer of a Lease Interest to Extend Lease
text:
Date: October 26, 2022

Written by: Emily Bergquist

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your client, [Taxpayer] regarding the applicability of property transfer tax to an assignment of lease and grant of options to renew. This ruling is based upon representations in your email dated [date].

Facts 

1. The [Church], (Church) as landlord, and [Initial Lessee] as tenant, entered into a ground lease dated June 10, 2010, for premises at [location], Vermont. The initial term of the ground lease is thirty years, beginning [date], and ending [date].

2. The ground lease provides the tenant one option to extend the lease term for ten years and a second option to extend the lease term for an additional 9 years and ten months. If both options were exercised the term of the ground lease would be 49 years and 10 months and would end on [date].

3. The ground lease does not contain an option for the tenant to purchase the leased premises.

4. By assignment dated [date], [Original Lessee] assigned its interest in the ground lease as tenant to [Assigned Lessee]. By assignment dated [date], [Assigned Lessee] assigned its interest in the ground lease to [Taxpayer].

You have asked the following questions:

Question 1: The remaining term of the ground lease, including the existing two options is approximately 37 years. If the ground lease were amended to provide the tenant with an additional option to extend the lease for a period of twelve years, which if exercised, would extend the lease to [date] October 31, 2071 (less than 50 years from now), would this amendment constitute a transfer of title to property under 32 V.S.A. Section 9601(3) requiring the payment of property transfer tax?

Question 2: If the ground lease were amended to provide tenant with options to extend the term of the ground lease beyond fifty years from the current date, would this amendment constitute a transfer of title to property under 32 V.S.A. Section 9601(3) requiring the payment of property transfer tax?

Question 3: If transfer tax is due under either of the above ground lease amendments, how would the transfer tax be calculated? Is it calculated on the gross rents due for the entire term of the ground lease, including extensions, without any present value discount or is it based on the fair market value of the leased premises?

Question 4: If the ground lease, following either of the amendments described above, was assigned by [Taxpayer] to a third party for consideration, would that assignment be subject to property transfer tax?

Discussion 

Property transfer tax is imposed on every transfer of title to property by deed or other writing. 32 V.S.A. § 9602. “Title to property” is defined as follows:

(3) "Title to property" includes:

(A) those interests in property that endure for a period of time the termination of which is not fixed or ascertained by a specific number of years, including an estate in fee simple, life estate, perpetual leasehold, and perpetual easement; and

(B) those interests in property enduring for a fixed period:

(i) equal to or exceeding 50 years;

(ii) less than 50 years if, by reason of a grant of right to extend the term by renewal or otherwise, said interest may be extended to a period equal to or exceeding 50 years;

(iii) less than 50 years if there is granted a right to purchase the property and there is granted the right to construct on the property a building or structure or to make such major capital improvements as water systems, sewer systems, roads, or parking facilities.

32 V.S.A. § 9601(3). A lease creates an “interest in property enduring for a fixed period.” If a lease is for a term or 50 years or longer, the transfer of that lease will be subject to transfer tax. If a lease is for a term of less than 50 years, but a right is granted to extend the lease term to a period equal to or exceeding 50 years from the date the right is granted, the grant of that right results in a transfer of an interest in property that will be subject to transfer tax.

An assignment of a lease is considered a “transfer” for purposes of the transfer tax:

(5) "Transfer" includes a grant, assignment, conveyance, will, trust, decree of court, transfer or acquisition of a direct or indirect controlling interest in any person with title to property, or any other means of transferring title to property or vesting title to property in any person.

32 V.S.A. § 9601(5).

In this case, [Church] granted an original lease to [Original Lessee] for a 30-year term, from [date] through [date], with no option to purchase. [Church] granted tenant [Original Lessee] an option to renew the lease for an additional 10 years, and granted [Original Lessee] an additional option to renew for another 9 years and 10 months, for a potential total lease term of 49 years and 10 months, ending [date]. [Church]’s transfer to [Original Lessee] was of an interest for a total of less than 50 years and therefore not subject to transfer tax. [Original Lessee] assigned that lease to [Assigned Lessee] in [year]. [Original Lessee]’s assignment to [Assigned Lessee] of the lease for a total of less than 50 years was also not subject to transfer tax.

[Assigned Lessee] then assigned the lease to [Taxpayer] in [year]. At that point, [Taxpayer] received a lease that ran from [year] through [year], a term of 23 years, plus option rights to extend the lease through [date], which would extend the lease to a potential term of 43 years, which is less than 50 years. [Assigned Lessee]’s assignment to [Taxpayer] was therefore also not subject to transfer tax.

Currently, [Taxpayer] holds a lease and rights to extend for a total of 37 years. If [Church] now grants [Taxpayer] an option to extend the lease for another 12 years, the term of the lease plus rights to extend would be 49 years (plus less than 2 months), through [date], a period of less than 50 years. The transfer of the new option would therefore not be subject to transfer tax.

If the new 12-year option to extend the lease is now granted to [Taxpayer] and [Taxpayer] then assigns the lease, the assignment would constitute a “transfer.” But since the term of the lease plus rights to extend to [year] would be less than 50 years, the assignment would not be subject to transfer tax.

If [Church] grants an option to extend the lease to a period that equals or exceeds fifty years from the date the option is granted, that grant would be subject to transfer tax.

Note that if there is any other written agreement that obligates [Church] to grant options to renew, that agreement would be considered part of the “transfer of title to property by deed or other writing.” The term of the promised options would be added to the lease-plus-current options to extend, and could result in a total potential lease term of 50 years or more, making the transfer taxable.

For purposes of the property transfer tax, the Department generally values leases using the total lease payments under the lease agreement including options to extend, adjusted to present value.

title: Ruling 2022-03: Exemption for Purchase of Building Materials to Construct or Alter Building Owned by Local Development Corporation
text:
Date: Not provided

Written by: Emily Bergquist

Approved by Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your client, [taxpayer], regarding the applicability of sales and use tax to purchases of building materials and supplies to be used in the acquisition and conversion of a former warehouse. This ruling is based upon representations in your letter dated [date], received in this office [date].

Facts 

The facts as you described them are as follows:

1. Your client, [Taxpayer] (Taxpayer), is a Vermont limited partnership.

2. [Corporation] is a Vermont nonprofit corporation, an exempt entity under Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (IRC), and a "local development corporation" as defined in 10 V.S.A. § 212(10)3. Taxpayer and [Corporation] will enter into a project to acquire the [location] in [town], a former [business type] warehouse, and then convert the building for mixed use with commercial tenants, including [tenant], and rental housing units.

3. Taxpayer and [Corporation] will enter into a project toc acquire the [location] in [town], a former [business type] warehouse, and then convert the building for mixed use with commercial tenants, including [tenant], and rental housing units.

4. [Corporation] will receive grants from [Commission], [Commission], [Board], and the [Town]. [Corporation] will receive a [Credit] awarded through the [Board] in accordance with 32 V.SA. §§ 5930aa - 5930ff.

5. [Corporation] "will acquire the fee interest" in the [location]. It is presumed for the purpose of this ruling that you use the quoted phrase to mean that [Corporation] will own the building.

Due to requirements under Federal income tax law in IRC §§ 42 and 47, governing Rehabilitation Tax Credits and Low-Income Housing Tax Credits, Taxpayer and [Corporation] intend to have [Corporation] lease the [location] to Taxpayer for a term of 99 years. [Corporation] will lend to Taxpayer funds from [Corporations]'s [Credit] award. Taxpayer will use these funds, plus capital contributions from its general and limited partners, plus proceeds from private loans, to pay for rehabilitation of the [location], including purchase of building

materials and supplies to be incorporated into the building.

7. You have asked whether Taxpayer's purchases of materials and supplies for use in the conversion of the [location] will be exempt from sales tax under 32 V.S.A. § 9743(4).

Discussion 

Vermont sales and use tax does not apply to the following:

(4) Sales of building materials and supplies to be used in the construction, reconstruction, alteration, remodeling, or repair of . . .

(C) any building or structure owned by any "local development corporation" as defined in 10 V.S.A. § 212(10), and used exclusively for the

purposes authorized in 10 V.S.A. Chapter 12; provided, however, that the . . . development corporation has first obtained a certificate from the Commissioner stating that it is entitled to the exemption and the vendor keeps a record of the sales price of each separate sale, the name of the purchaser, the date of each separate sale, and the number of the certificate.

32 V.S.A. § 9743(4). For an eligible project, this exemption covers purchases of the following:

In this subdivision, the words "building materials and supplies" shall include all materials and supplies consumed, employed, or expended in the construction, reconstruction, alteration, remodeling, or repair of any building, structure, or other public work as well as the materials and supplies physically incorporated therein.

32 V.S.A. § 9743(4)(C).

Under Subsection (C) of Subsection 9743(4), quoted above, the sales tax exemption applies only to materials and supplies used in altering a building owned by a "local development corporation" as defined in Title 10 and "used exclusively for the purposes authorized in Chapter 12 of Title 10." In addition, the exemption is available only if the local development corporation first obtains exemption certification from the Commissioner of Taxes, and only if each vendor of the materials and supplies keeps records of each sale as required by Subdivision (C).

In Taxpayer's case, the ruling request letter states that the building to be altered will be owned by [Corporation] and that [Corporation] is a "local Development corporation" as defined in Title 10. Thus, the first requirement for the sales tax exemption is met.

The [location] will, however, not be "used exclusively for the purposes authorized in chapter 12 of Title 10." The relevant "purposes authorized in Chapter 12" of Title 10 are found in Sections 210 and 212 of thx chapter. Section 210 states:

§ 210. Statutory purposes 

The statutory purpose of the exemption for local development corporations in Section 236 of this title is to promote economic development. 10 V.S.A. § 210. This broad statement of purpose is narrowed by the definition of "eligible project" in Section 212:

(6) "Eligible facility" or "eligible project" means any industrial, commercial, or agricultural enterprise or endeavor approved by the Authority that meets the criteria established in the Vermont Sustainable Jobs Strategy adopted by the Governor under section 280b of this title, including land and rights in land, air, or water, buildings, structures, machinery, and equipment of such eligible facilities or eligible projects, except that an eligible facility or project shall not include the portion of an enterprise or endeavor relating to the sale of goods at retail where such goods are manufactured primarily out of state, and except further that an eligible facility or project shall not include the portion of an enterprise or endeavor relating to housing. 

10 V.S.A. § 212(6).

Since the [location] will be altered for commercial tenants, but also to provide rental housing units, the building will not be "used exclusively for the purposes authorized in chapter 12 of Title 10." The portion of the [location] used for housing will not meet the second requirement for the sales tax exemption and thus will not be eligible for the exemption.

It is not stated whether any commercial tenant of the [location] will sell "at retail . . . goods . . . manufactured primarily out of state." Any portion of the building to be used for retail of such goods would also not be eligible for the sales tax exemption.

As noted earlier, the sales tax exemption only applies to purchases made after the local development corporation "has first obtained a certificate from the Commissioner stating that it is entitled to the exemption." Taxpayer may obtain the Commissioner's certification by request from the Taxpayer Services Division at the Department. Taxpayer may then complete Form S-3C, which is the exemption certificate for "Contractors Completing a Qualified Exempt Project." Taxpayer must present the completed Form S-3C to its sellers at the time it purchases the building materials and supplies for the eligible portion of this project.
